title: “I DON’T KNOW HIM.”
paragraphs:
Three words.
Sharp as a knife.
Spoken beside a fire that was warming the hands of a man whose heart was freezing.
Simon Peter — the loudest voice of loyalty hours earlier — now whispers denial in the dark.
The courtyard smelled like smoke and fear.

The torches flickered.
Soldiers laughed somewhere in the shadows.
The trial of Jesus Christ was unfolding inside the house of Caiaphas.
A fisherman was fighting a different trial.
Just hours earlier, Peter had made a promise recorded in Gospel of Luke 22.
“Lord, I am ready to go with you to prison and to death.”
But Jesus had already spoken the prophecy:
“Before the rooster crows today, you will deny three times that you know me.”
A servant girl squinted through the firelight.
“I DON’T KNOW WHAT YOU’RE TALKING ABOUT!”
A sound cut through the cold air.
At that moment, Jesus Christ turned and looked at Peter.
A look that pierced deeper than judgment.
The sound of a heart collapsing under the weight of its own failure.
Peter did not just make a mistake.
He denied the One he swore to die for.
This is not the end of Peter’s story.
Because the Gospel does something scandalous with failure.
After the resurrection, on another shoreline fire, Jesus Christ will ask Peter three times:
Grace does not erase the past.

The man who said, “I don’t know Him”…
will later stand in Jerusalem and preach Christ so boldly that thousands believe.
That is the mercy of the cross.
You didn’t deny Jesus with words.

But with silence.
With compromise.
With secret sin.
You warmed your hands at the wrong fire.
Failure is not final when Christ is involved.

The same Savior Peter denied
went to the cross to forgive deniers like us.

Sin exposed.
Grace extended.
Redemption secured by the blood of Jesus.
If Peter’s story proves anything, it’s this:
Your worst moment does not get the last word.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
